column1: # How people actually type Persian in Latin letters ("Finglish" / "Pinglish"),
# and what they mean by it. Nothing here is reachable from the phonetic rules,
# because the Persian script throws away what the rules would need:
#  - short vowels, which it does not write at all, so only a dictionary knows
#    whether an "a" is a long ا or nothing ("kar" is کار but "dars" درس);
#  - the Arabic letters Persian keeps for its loanwords, which sound the same
#    as the native ones: ح against ه ("hala" is حالا), ص ث against س ("sobh"
#    is صبح), ط against ت ("chetori" چطوری), ذ ض ظ against ز ("ghaza" غذا,
#    "zohr" ظهر), غ against ق ("ghalat" غلط) and the silent ع ("eshgh" عشق);
#  - آ against ا at the start of a word ("are" is آره, "alan" الان), and the
#    silent و of خوا ("khab" is خواب, "mikham" می‌خوام);
#  - the verb prefix می / نمی, which Persian joins to the stem with a ZWNJ
#    (U+200C) rather than a space: "midoonam" is می‌دونم. The ZWNJ inside a
#    value is part of the word, not a space.
# Spellings are the colloquial (Tehrani) ones people chat in, the way the fa
# word list writes them: خونه, می‌دونم, اومدم, not the literary خانه, می‌دانم,
# آمدم (a few literary forms are kept as second choices). Chat shorthand is
# here too: "slm" for سلام, "mrc" for مرسی, "khdfz" for خدافظ, "dg" for دیگه.
# Lines the rules already get right are left out. A spelling may repeat to
# offer alternatives, preferred first ("khob" is خب, then خوب; "bad" is بد,
# then بعد). It is a draft written without a native speaker and wants a
